title: Release script dies on the export gate's aborted push
description:
## Summary

`pnpm run release <bump>` strands the release: it commits the version bump and then dies before
tagging, leaving the two manifests at the new version with no tag and nothing pushed. This happened
to v0.5.2, which sat committed-but-untagged on local main until the tag was pushed by hand.

## Problem

The release script and the bead export gate have contradictory contracts, and the release script
loses.

`scripts/beadsExportGate.ts` runs from `.beads/hooks/pre-push`. On main, when the committed
`.beads/issues.jsonl` differs from a fresh export, it commits the refresh on its own and returns 1
to abort the push, printing "nothing was pushed - run the push again". A pre-push hook cannot amend
the refs git has already computed, so that second push is the design, not a failure.

`scripts/release.ts` does not push again. Its `git()` helper (`release.ts:44`) calls `execFileSync`
with piped stdio, so the aborted push throws an uncaught exception and the gate's explanation is
swallowed into a buffer nobody reads. The script dies at `release.ts:182`, before `git tag`
(`release.ts:187`).

Evidence from the v0.5.2 attempt, reflog timestamps to the second:

- `02:14:18` `Release v0.5.2` — the release script's commit
- `02:14:20` `chore(beads): refresh the issues export` — the gate's commit, two seconds later
- no `v0.5.2` tag, nothing pushed

This recurs on essentially every release. Cutting a release follows bead work — claim, update,
close — so the export is stale by the time the release commit lands. v0.5.1 got through only
because the export happened to be current.

Re-running after the failure makes it worse rather than resuming: the manifests are clean at the
already-bumped version, so a second `release maintenance` bumps again and the stranded version is
never released.

Two consequences worth designing around rather than fighting:

- The gate's commit always lands between the release commit and the tag, so the tag can never sit
  on the `Release vX` commit while the gate runs after the bump.
- The release script has no test coverage at all, unlike `beadsExportGate.ts` and `diskPreflight.ts`
  which are both tested.

## Scope

- Make `pnpm run release` survive the export gate so a release run ends tagged and pushed.
- Make git failures inside the release script legible instead of an uncaught `execFileSync` stack
  trace — a rejected push, a hook that stood in the way, a missing credential should each say so.
- Cover the new behaviour with tests, in the shape `beadsExportGate.ts` and `diskPreflight.ts`
  already use: the decision logic split from the doing, so the cases are testable without pushing.

Two approaches, to be decided with the navigator when the bead is worked:

1. Retry the push once. The gate is a no-op the second time. Smallest change; leaves the tag on the
   gate's commit.
2. Push once before the bump, so the gate fires while nothing is at stake, and the release commit
   and its tag stay adjacent. Slightly more moving parts, better end state.

## Out of scope

- Changing the export gate's behaviour. Its "push again" contract is deliberate and documented; the
  release script is what must accommodate it.
- The `main` ruleset (10 required status checks, admin-only bypass). It is a separate concern that
  will reject this same push for a non-admin token, but it is not what broke v0.5.2.
- Any rework of the release GitHub workflow itself.

## Validation

- `pnpm run release maintenance --dry-run` with a deliberately stale `.beads/issues.jsonl` on main:
  the run completes rather than dying at the push.
- A full release run from main with a stale export ends with the tag pushed and origin/main
  carrying both the release commit and the gate's refresh commit.
- `pnpm run test:tooling` covers the new logic.
- The failure paths report their cause: point the script at an unpushable remote and confirm the
  message names the push rather than printing a stack trace.
acceptance_criteria: A release run from main with a stale .beads/issues.jsonl ends with the version commit pushed and the tag pushed, rather than stopping at the commit; a git failure inside release.ts reports what failed instead of an uncaught execFileSync stack trace; the new logic is covered by tests under pnpm run test:tooling

title: cargoTargetDir's worktree check fails whenever pnpm check runs from a worktree
description:
`scripts/cargoTargetDir.test.ts` derives the repository root from its own file location (`scripts/..`). Run from a git worktree that is what it gets - `.claude/worktrees/<name>` - so `git worktree list` then reports the main checkout and every sibling worktree as strays, and the test fails:

    expected [ '/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud',
               '/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/.claude/worktrees/pr75' ] to deeply equal []

CI never sees it, because a CI checkout has no worktrees. It bites locally, and it bites in the one workflow this repository actually prescribes: CLAUDE.md has agents work in `.claude/worktrees/`, where `pnpm check` now stops at `pnpm test` before it reaches the smoke suite. Hit while merging ah-ebv (#144); the whole remaining gate had to be run by hand, step by step.

The property the test is defending is right - a worktree outside the repository silently gets its own target directory and its own empty bead database. It is the anchor that is wrong: the root should come from git (`git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, then up one from `.git`) rather than from where the test file happens to sit, so the check asks the same question wherever it is run from.

## Validation

- `pnpm run test:tooling` passes from a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` and from the main checkout alike.
- A control: a worktree created outside the repository is still reported as a stray, so the test has not simply been widened into always passing.
acceptance_criteria:
pnpm run test:tooling passes when run from a worktree under .claude/worktrees/, and from the main checkout.
The repository root is taken from git rather than from the test file's own path.
A worktree genuinely outside the repository still fails the check, pinned by a test.
notes:
Raised to P1 on 2026-08-13 after hitting it a second time, while gating ah-ctf (#149).

What the description does not yet record, and what makes this worse than a noisy check: pnpm run test is an && chain -

  pnpm -r run test && pnpm run test:tooling && cargo test --workspace

test:tooling is the failing link, so cargo test --workspace never runs at all. An agent who reads the failure as 'unrelated tooling test' and moves on has silently skipped the entire Rust suite while believing the gate covered it. On ah-ctf the 576 Rust tests only ran because the short-circuit was noticed and cargo test was invoked separately.

So the cost is not only the manual gate the description mentions. It is a gate that looks broader than it is, in the exact direction - Rust - that the TypeScript suites cannot cover. Worth considering as part of the fix whether the chain should keep going and report every failure rather than stopping at the first.

title: Instructions for the two agent roles
description:
Two documents have to agree before either skill ships, because CLAUDE.md is always loaded and a skill that contradicts it resolves unpredictably - some sessions stall waiting for the navigator, some merge and are in violation.

- The Four Eye Principle in .github/copilot-instructions.md currently says no automatic merging is allowed and that the navigator must approve every PR. It is amended to name the Copilot reviewer as the second pair of eyes for bead-implemented PRs, with its conditions: every mandatory plan section present, every review thread resolved against the final head, and every check green.
- The beads-workflow skill gains the planned / human / needs-ui-decision lifecycle and its two atomic pickups.
- The never-reclaim rule, written when nothing heartbeated, is narrowed: a scoped bd reclaim --older-than 15m --label planned is allowed now that agents heartbeat, paired with pruning the dead agent's worktree.
acceptance_criteria:
CLAUDE.md and the beads-workflow skill agree with each other and with the two new skills on merging, claiming and reclaiming.
The label lifecycle is documented in one place and referenced from the others.
The narrowed reclaim rule says what makes a stale lease meaningful now and what it still does not license.

title: The plan-bead and implement-bead skills
description:
The two skills themselves: .claude/skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/implement-bead/SKILL.md, invoked as /plan-bead and /implement-bead in their own sessions. Committed automatically under the existing .gitignore rule that shares .claude/skills/.

The planner states its required model (Fable, else Opus, high effort) and declines to run on anything else - a skill cannot set the session model, but it can refuse. It claims with bd ready --exclude-label planned --claim, researches, takes architecture decisions itself, discusses every UI decision with the navigator over self-contained HTML mockups, writes the plan to the design field, labels it planned and unclaims.

The implementer claims with bd ready --label planned --claim, works in .claude/worktrees/<bead-id>, runs TDD under standing pre-approval, and waits for a Copilot review whose commit.oid equals the current head - never for an approval, which never comes.
acceptance_criteria:
Both skills exist, are invocable as /plan-bead and /implement-bead, and are committed.
The planner refuses to run on the wrong model and never plans a UI bead unattended.
The implementer refuses a plan missing a mandatory section and hands the bead back in one command.
The review wait keys on commit.oid matching the head SHA, and re-requests review after pushing fixes.
notes:
Traps for the implement-bead skill, found by running the loop:

1. The smoke suite rebuilds apps/web/dist with ATLANTIS_PWA_DISABLE=1, so running test:pwa after test:smoke without rebuilding fails with page timeouts and no service worker. pnpm check orders it build:web then test:pwa for exactly this reason. An agent that meets this unattended will plausibly go and 'fix' the service worker.

2. Never arm 'gh pr merge --auto' before the review round is closed. Auto-merge fires on green checks alone: it does not wait for a review, and it races any fix pushed afterwards. On #142 it merged the pre-review head and --delete-branch then removed the branch carrying the fixes, which survived only in the local object store.

3. Expect BEHIND on nearly every merge. With the strict up-to-date rule and several agents merging, a PR that sat through one review round is usually behind main, and each rebase costs a full CI cycle. Rebase, re-run the local gate, force-with-lease.

4. Copilot reviews roughly four PRs in five, sometimes minutes late, and never approves - every review is COMMENTED. Wait on a review whose commit.oid equals the current head, re-request after every push, and bound the wait.
Merge discipline, decided with the navigator after four of five PRs each needed an extra rebase and full CI cycle purely because another agent merged during review:

Keep the strict branches-up-to-date rule and rebase every time. A green gate on a stale tree is evidence about a tree that will never exist, and two agents changing the same function compatibly - both green, broken on main - is exactly what the rule catches. No merge queue for now.

The skill must state the cost plainly rather than let each agent rediscover it: expect BEHIND on most merges, budget a rebase plus a full CI cycle per review round, and never treat the rebase as optional. Revisit if the agent count grows past three or so.

title: Protect main so red or stale work cannot merge
description:
gh api reports main is not protected: no ruleset, no required checks, and allow_auto_merge is false. So 'CI must be green' would be enforced only by an agent reading gh pr checks correctly - and every known misreading (a pending check taken as passed, a queued job ignored, a green-but-stale branch) lands straight on main with no backstop. This is the single largest false-green lever in the harness.

A ruleset on main requires the CI job names with branches-up-to-date, auto-merge is enabled, and the agent's merge step becomes gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch --auto: GitHub then owns waiting, ordering and staleness, and the agent's attempt budget becomes a give-up rule rather than a merge-permission rule.

The navigator is a bypass actor. This is a settings change on a live repository and needs the navigator to make it or to approve the exact gh api calls.
acceptance_criteria:
A ruleset on main requires the CI job names and branches to be up to date.
Auto-merge is enabled on the repository.
The navigator is a bypass actor; agent PRs are not exempt.
A deliberately red PR cannot be merged by the documented agent command.
notes: Amended after review with the navigator: a bypass actor was added (RepositoryRole 5, admin, bypass_mode always). Verified by probe - a direct push to main is now permitted with a '10 of 10 required status checks are expected' warning rather than declined. The trade is explicit: agents authenticate with the navigator's token and hold admin, so they inherit the bypass. The ruleset therefore stops accidents (red or stale merges through the PR path, force-pushes, branch deletion) but is not a hard guarantee against an agent that merges deliberately. That guarantee, if wanted later, needs a separate identity for agents.
close_reason: Ruleset 20771276 active on main: 10 required checks, strict up-to-date, no bypass; auto-merge enabled. Verified by a rejected direct push.

title: One cargo build directory, and a disk preflight
description:
There is no .cargo/config.toml, so every git worktree builds its own target tree: 10G + 2.7G + 5.8G for one repository, on a disk that was at 100% capacity with 2.0 GiB free when this was found. Each further implementation agent adds another 3-6 GB, and cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets is the biggest of them.

The failure mode is an ENOSPC part-way through a build, which surfaces as a strange linker or codegen error that an agent will try to fix in code.

A committed .cargo/config.toml points every worktree at one shared build directory outside the repo. The per-worktree target trees then become dead weight and can be removed. An implementation agent refuses to start a bead when free space is under a threshold, rather than discovering it mid-build.
acceptance_criteria:
A committed .cargo/config.toml sets a shared build.target-dir outside the repository.
The obsolete per-worktree target trees are removed and the space is measurably reclaimed.
The implement skill refuses to create a worktree below a stated free-space threshold, naming the real cause.

title: Per-agent ports for the smoke and PWA suites
description:
playwright.config.ts pins 4173/4174 and playwright.pwa.config.ts pins 4175. Concurrent agents collide.

The PWA config is the dangerous one: its preview command has no --strictPort, so a second agent's Vite quietly falls back to 4176 while Playwright's readiness probe hits 4175 and finds the FIRST agent's server. Every PWA test then passes against someone else's bundle. The smoke config is safe only by luck, because it does pass --strictPort.

Both configs take a port base from an env var, defaulting to today's numbers so a plain local run is unchanged, and --strictPort is added to the PWA preview so a collision is always loud.
acceptance_criteria:
Both configs derive their ports from an env-provided base, defaulting to 4173/4174/4175.
The PWA preview command passes --strictPort.
Port resolution is a pure function with tests under the tooling vitest config.
Two agents run test:smoke and test:pwa simultaneously and pass against their own bundles; breaking one worktree's source reddens only that agent's run.

title: Export gate stands aside off main
description:
scripts/beadsExportGate.ts writes the whole bead database into .beads/issues.jsonl on every branch it runs on. Two agents' PRs therefore carry complete backlog snapshots taken at different moments, and whichever merges last silently reverts every close, claim, label and plan recorded in between. Git usually will not even conflict, because each side rewrote a different subset of the one-line-per-bead file.

The gate becomes a main-only obligation: on any other branch it stands aside, exactly as it already does when bd is missing or node_modules are absent. main is refreshed by the planner's own pushes and by a post-merge refresh.

This is the highest-probability silent-wrong-result in the harness, and it gets worse once plans live in the design field.
acceptance_criteria:
runGate proceeds without exporting when the current branch is not main.
The existing stand-aside idiom and its tests are followed rather than a new mechanism.
Two branches, each pushed after a bead change and merged in turn, leave the first branch's bead state intact - demonstrated, not assumed.

title: Planner and implementer agent harness
description:
A planning session turns unplanned beads into fully specified ones and owns every UI decision with the navigator; one or more implementation sessions pick up a planned bead, implement it under TDD, get it reviewed by Copilot, merged, and loop.

The split only works if the plan is a real contract and if the agents cannot corrupt each other. A stress test against this repository found five ways the obvious design breaks or silently produces wrong results; the infrastructure children below are those fixes, and they must land before more than one implementation agent runs.

Full design, including the twenty decisions taken with the navigator, is in the children's plans and in the harness skills themselves.
acceptance_criteria:
One planner session and one implementer session carry a real bead from unplanned to merged, with no navigator action beyond the UI discussion during planning.
Two agents can run the smoke and PWA suites at once without testing each other's bundles.
Concurrent PRs no longer overwrite each other's bead state.

title: Stop agents colliding on a bead someone already claimed
description:
## Summary

Two agents keep starting work on the same bead. The cause is not carelessness — it is that a claim
looks abandoned within minutes of being taken.

`bd update <id> --claim` takes a **lease** with a short TTL, kept alive only by `bd heartbeat`.
Neither `CLAUDE.md` nor the `beads-workflow` skill mentions `bd heartbeat` at all, so no agent here
has ever sent one. A work cycle in this repo — RED, GREEN, REFACTOR, a full local gate, CI — runs an
hour or more against a TTL of roughly five minutes.

Observed, on a bead an agent had claimed ten minutes earlier and was demonstrably still working
(it had already wired a dependency from it):

```
◐ ah-xde · Remove the Classic map theme   [P2 · IN_PROGRESS]
Lease: expires in 1 min (heartbeat 3 mins ago)
```

`bd reclaim` is the reaper: it finds in_progress issues whose lease expired, **clears the assignee
and sets them back to open** so another worker can claim them. `bd update --force` documents itself
as being for "abandoned claims — crashed agent, expired lease". With nobody heartbeating, every live
claim in this repository matches that description exactly.

Three contributing findings:

- **The selection window.** The loop claims before branching, but exploration and planning happen
  first — one bead was planned for ten minutes before it was claimed. Selected-but-unclaimed work is
  invisible to every other agent.
- **Worktrees are not the problem.** All three worktrees resolve to the same Dolt database, so a
  claim is visible locally the moment it is written.
- **Cross-machine is.** Leases are node-local and write no Dolt commit; only status and assignee
  commit, and those travel only on `bd dolt push`/`bd dolt pull`. The skill says to push at session
  end, so a claim can stay invisible to another machine for an entire session.

`claim.ttl` is not a documented config key — `bd config get claim.ttl` reports "not set", and the
skill already records that `bd config set` accepts unknown keys silently — so lengthening the TTL is
not a reliable lever. The fix belongs in the instructions.

## Scope

Update `.claude/skills/beads-workflow/SKILL.md` and `CLAUDE.md` (the symlink to
`.github/copilot-instructions.md`) with four rules, agreed with the navigator:

1. **Claim first.** `bd update <id> --claim` is the first action after choosing a bead — before
   exploring, planning or asking questions, not merely before branching. A failed claim means
   somebody else won; pick another bead.
2. **Heartbeat while working.** `bd heartbeat <id>` at every phase gate and before any long wait (a
   full smoke run, a CI watch). Heartbeats write no Dolt commit and no history, so the cadence is
   free.
3. **Never take over a claim unasked.** `in_progress` with an assignee is authoritative whatever the
   lease says. No `bd reclaim`, no `bd update --force`, no reassignment over a live claim without
   the navigator saying so — an expired lease here means "nobody heartbeated", not "the worker
   died".
4. **Push the claim immediately.** `bd dolt push` right after claiming, not only at session end, so
   another machine can see it. Keep the session-end push as well.

Record the lease behaviour itself in the skill's Traps section, so an agent that meets a stale lease
recognises it rather than reasoning from `--force`'s help text.

## Out of scope

- Changing `claim.ttl` or any beads configuration; the key is not part of the documented surface.
- A supervisor process running `bd reclaim` on a timer. That is the upstream design for dead-worker
  recovery, and it is exactly what must not run here while nothing heartbeats.

## Validation

- `bd heartbeat <id>` on a bead this session holds, confirming the lease moves forward — the one
  claim in the four rules that has never actually been exercised here.
- Re-read both documents end to end: the daily loop, the checklist and CLAUDE.md's work-package
  rules must agree with each other, since all three currently describe claiming.
- No code changes, so the gate is `pnpm run lint` for the markdown-adjacent tooling only.
acceptance_criteria:
The beads-workflow skill and CLAUDE.md both say to claim before exploring or planning, not merely before branching.
Both say to heartbeat during long work, naming bd heartbeat.
Both forbid bd reclaim, bd update --force and reassignment over a live claim without the navigator's approval.
Both say to bd dolt push straight after claiming, in addition to at session end.
The skill's Traps section explains the lease TTL and why an expired lease here does not mean an abandoned worker.

title: A view for reading the turn's battles
description:
## Summary

A view that lists the battles of the loaded turn and shows one in full.

## Problem

Once ah-1is.1 lands, the battles are in the model and still nowhere on screen.

## Scope

- A list of the turn's battles, each line answering who fought whom, where, and the outcome in
  casualties, so a player can see at a glance whether the turn went well.
- Opening one shows it in full: both rosters, the rounds in order with their spells and loss
  lines, total casualties, damaged units and the spoils.
- The location links back to the map — selecting a battle should be able to take the player to
  the hex it happened in, the way the turn-messages panel takes them to a unit
  (`onSelectUnit`, `packages/shared/src/workspace/TurnMessagesPanel.tsx:39`).
- Units that are the player's own should be distinguishable from everyone else's in the
  rosters. The parsed unit model already carries `own`
  (`crates/core/src/report/model.rs:104-107`) for units in regions; if the battle roster does not
  give enough to decide, match on faction id and say plainly when it cannot be told.
- Round statistics arrive as text (see ah-1is.1). Show them, but folded away by default — they
  are hundreds of lines and would bury the rounds themselves.

**Shape.** Every faction- or turn-scoped surface today is a header chip with a popover
(`TurnMessagesPanel`, `ProblemsPanel`, `MergedFactionsPanel`, mounted from
`packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx:2027-2105`); all five collapsible panels are
hex- or unit-scoped. A battle in full is much larger than any of those popovers hold, so this
one probably wants a chip that opens something bigger — a dialog, or a list in the popover that
opens the full battle elsewhere. Put the options to the navigator before building, as the
faction view bead (ah-vp3) does.

## Out of scope

- Anything the parser does not provide (see ah-1is.1: round statistics stay as text).
- Comparing battles across turns.

## Validation

- `pnpm test` — component tests over the list and the full view, including a turn with no
  battles.
- `pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck`
- A smoke test in `tests/smoke/` covering opening a battle from the header, in the style of the
  existing turn-messages coverage.
- Manual: import `tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-f95-t71.rep`, open the second battle
  (`Sail (16352)` attacks `Looter (16779)` in `ocean (26,52)`), and check the casualties and
  spoils against the report text.
acceptance_criteria: The turn's battles are listed with participants, location and casualties; opening one shows both rosters, the rounds in order, total casualties, damaged units and spoils; the battle's hex can be reached from the view; round statistics are available but folded away by default; a turn with no battles shows an empty state rather than breaking

title: Parse the battles of the turn report
description:
## Summary

Parse the `Battles during turn:` section into a structured model and expose it to the
TypeScript side, so a view can be built on it.

## Problem

The section is skipped outright (`crates/core/src/report/header.rs:151`). Nothing downstream
can see a battle.

## Scope

**Where it goes.** The battles sit inside the preamble slice `parse_header` is given —
everything before the first region block (`crates/core/src/report/mod.rs:94`) — and today's
real-report tests pass, which proves no battle line is mistaken for a region header. Put the
parsing in a new `crates/core/src/report/battle.rs` rather than growing `header.rs`, and have
`parse_header` hand the section to it.

**Splitting the section into battles.** `unwrap_lines` drops blank lines
(`crates/core/src/report/unwrap.rs:85`), so blocks cannot be split on them. Split on the
headline instead — `<unit> (<id>) attacks <unit> (<id>) in <terrain> (<x>,<y>) in <province>!` —
and treat everything up to the next headline (or the end of the preamble) as that battle.
Assassinations print a different headline; recognise what is recognisable and keep the rest as
text rather than dropping a block that does not match.

**The model.** Per battle:

- The headline: attacker and defender unit names and ids, and the location as terrain,
  coordinate and province, so the UI can point at the hex on the map.
- Attacker and defender rosters, one entry per unit: name, id, owning faction where printed,
  flags, and the item/skill body. Parsing the body down to individual items is *not* required
  here — a unit line already has a shape `crates/core/src/report/unit.rs` understands, so reuse
  what fits and keep the remainder verbatim rather than inventing a second unit parser.
- The rounds in order: the round's lines (tactics bonuses, spells, "breathes Fire, killing 15")
  and the per-side loss lines that close it.
- Total casualties per side, the damaged-unit ids, and the spoils.
- `line_start`/`line_end` from `LogicalLine` for the block, so the verbatim report text can be
  recovered for display.

**Round statistics.** The `Round N statistics:` blocks are the bulk of the section — hundreds of
per-unit, per-weapon tallies. Keep them as text attached to their round for now; do not model
them field by field. If that turns out to be wanted, it is a separate bead.

**Tolerance.** A report with no battles parses to an empty list. A battle missing a section
(no spoils line, no statistics) parses with that part empty. Nothing here may make a report fail
to parse.

**Boundary.** Add the battles to `ReportHeader` (or alongside it in `ParsedReport` — the
implementer's call, but say which and why in the PR) and mirror the type in
`packages/core-client/src/index.ts` next to `ReportHeaderInfo` (index.ts:391). Both adapters
serialise `ParsedReport` straight through with `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`
(`crates/core-wasm/src/lib.rs:648`, `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs:458`), so the hand-written
TypeScript mirror is the only part that can drift.

**Size.** A parsed turn is persisted, so measure what this adds to a stored turn before
finishing. If keeping the statistics text doubles the record, say so on the bead and propose
dropping it to the navigator rather than deciding alone.

## Out of scope

- Any UI. That is the sibling bead.
- Battles from merged allied reports (see the parent, ah-1is).
- Modelling the round statistics field by field.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p atlantis-core` — unit tests over a hand-written minimal battle, plus the real
  fixture `tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-f95-t71.rep`: two battles, the first
  `AA Tomb's Guards (7280)` attacking `Pirates (14789)` in `ocean (25,55)` in `Atlantis Ocean`,
  one round, `Pirates (14789) loses 15`, `AA Tomb's Guards (7280) loses 0`, damaged unit 14789,
  and spoils ending `2531 silver [SILV]`.
- A test that the other fixtures, which have no battles, still parse to an empty list and are
  otherwise unchanged.
- `pnpm test && pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck` for the boundary types.
acceptance_criteria: The Battles during turn section parses into an ordered list of battles, each with participants, location (terrain, coordinate, province), attacker and defender rosters, rounds with their loss lines, total casualties, damaged unit ids, spoils, and the source line span; the f95 turn-71 fixture yields its two battles with the values named in Validation; reports without battles parse to an empty list and are otherwise unchanged; the battles reach the TypeScript side through both adapters

title: See the battles of the turn
description:
## Summary

See every battle the turn report describes: who fought whom and where, how each side was made
up, what the rounds did, who died and what was taken.

## Problem

Battles are the part of a turn a player most wants to re-read, and they are the one large
section of the report the app throws away. `parse_header` names `"Battles during turn"` only to
skip it (`crates/core/src/report/header.rs:151`), so every battle line falls on the floor
without a warning — which is the parser's tolerant contract working as intended, but it means
the only way to read a battle is to open the `.rep` file in a text editor and scroll.

The section is not small. In `tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-f95-t71.rep` the battles
run from line 57 to roughly line 1930 — most of the file — and hold two battles, each with:

```
AA Tomb's Guards (7280) attacks Pirates (14789) in ocean (25,55) in
  Atlantis Ocean!

Attackers:      <roster: unit, faction, flags, men, items, skills>
Defenders:      <roster>
Round 1:        <tactics bonuses, spells cast, "breathes Fire, killing 15">
                <side> loses <n>.
Round 1 statistics:   <per-unit, per-weapon attack tallies>
Total Casualties:
Pirates (14789) loses 15.
Damaged units: 14789.
Spoils: 3 magic crossbows [MXBO], ... 2531 silver [SILV].
```

## Scope

Two children, in order:

1. Parse the battle blocks in the core and carry them across the boundary.
2. A view in the workspace that lists the turn's battles and shows one in full.

## Out of scope

- Battles from merged allied reports. `merge_report_into_sightings`
  (`crates/core/src/report/merge.rs:135`) merges regions and sightings only; headers are not
  merged at all, so an ally's battles would need a deduplication story of their own. Worth doing
  later, deliberately, rather than falling out of this work by accident.
- Any simulation, prediction or replay of combat. This is reading what happened.
- Battle history across turns; that belongs with ah-jg6.
acceptance_criteria: Every battle in the loaded turn report can be read in the app: the participants, where it happened, each side's roster, the rounds, the casualties and the spoils

title: See faction-level information: attitudes, allowances and unclaimed silver
description:
## Summary

Somewhere to see the faction as a whole: who we have declared what towards, how much of our
region and mage allowances is spent, and how much silver is sitting unclaimed.

## Problem

The report says all of this and the app shows none of it. Two blocks of the preamble are read
past today:

```
Faction Status:
Regions: 3 (10)
Quartermasters: 0 (0)
Mages: 6 (6)
Apprentices: 0 (15)
...
Declared Attitudes (default Unfriendly):
Hostile : Creatures (2), The Guardsmen (1), Dark League (28), ...
Neutral : Fon (8).
Friendly : The Gaggle (22), Kiiran (3), ...
Ally : Wistful Thinking (27), ...
```

`parse_header` names `"Faction Status"` only to skip it
(`crates/core/src/report/header.rs:151`) and never looks at attitudes at all — the only mention
of attitudes in the core is the DECLARE order grammar (`crates/core/src/orders/grammar.rs:68`),
which is the writing side, not the reading side.

Unclaimed silver *is* parsed (`crates/core/src/report/header.rs:48`) and does reach the
TypeScript side as `ReportHeaderInfo.unclaimedSilver`
(`packages/core-client/src/index.ts:401`), but nothing renders it; the same is true of
`factionTypes`. Both are referenced only by test fixtures.

So "am I at my region limit?", "can I train another apprentice?", "is this faction an ally?" and
"how much have I forgotten to CLAIM?" all mean going back to the report text.

## Scope

**Parsing** — `crates/core/src/report/header.rs`

- Read the `Faction Status:` block into structured counts of used-of-maximum. Keep it
  key-agnostic rather than hard-coding four fields: NewOrigins prints `Regions`, standard
  Atlantis prints `Tax Regions` and `Trade Regions`, and a ruleset may print others. An
  unrecognised line should be carried, not dropped.
- Read `Declared Attitudes (default <X>):` into the default attitude plus, per attitude level,
  the factions declared at it (name and id). Entries wrap across lines; `unwrap_lines` already
  joins continuations, so the parser should see one logical line per attitude — confirm that
  against the real fixture rather than assuming it.
- Both blocks fall inside the preamble slice `parse_header` is given (everything before the
  first region block, `crates/core/src/report/mod.rs:94`), so the preamble boundary needs no
  change.
- Stay tolerant, as the rest of the parser is: a report without either block parses fine and
  leaves the fields empty.

**Boundary**

- Extend `ReportHeader` / `ReportHeaderInfo` with the new data and carry it through the wasm and
  Tauri adapters. Both serialise `ParsedReport` straight through with
  `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` (`crates/core-wasm/src/lib.rs:648`,
  `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs:458`), so the TypeScript mirror in
  `packages/core-client/src/index.ts:391` is the only hand-written part to keep in step.

**UI**

- A faction view showing: faction name, id and types; unclaimed silver; the status counts as
  used-of-maximum; and the declared attitudes grouped by level with the default stated.
- All five collapsible panels are hex- or unit-scoped; every faction-scoped surface today is a
  header chip with a popover under it (`MergedFactionsPanel`, `TurnMessagesPanel`). The header
  already renders `Faction <name>` with the merged-factions chip hanging off it
  (`packages/shared/src/workspace/AppHeader.tsx`), so making that the trigger for an anchored
  panel — dismissed on Escape and on an outside press, as `TurnMessagesPanel` does — fits better
  than a sixth dock panel: this is read occasionally, not watched while planning. Confirm the
  shape with the navigator before building it.
- Where a faction in the attitude lists is one whose report has been merged in, say so. Do not
  invent links to factions the app knows nothing about.

## Out of scope

- Writing or editing `DECLARE` orders from the view — reading only, for now.
- How attitudes and allowances changed since last turn; that belongs with ah-jg6.
- Any faction-level statistic the report does not state (income totals, item tallies).

## Validation

- `cargo test -p atlantis-core` — unit tests for both blocks, plus the real-report fixtures
  `tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-f95-t71.rep` (attitudes at every level, wrapped
  entries, `Regions: 0 (0)`) and `...-f73-t71.rep` (`Regions: 3 (10)`, `Apprentices: 0 (15)`).
- `pnpm test && pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck`
- Manual: import f95 turn 71 and check the view against the report text — 6038 unclaimed silver,
  6 of 6 mages, 15 of 15 apprentices, default Unfriendly, Fon (8) neutral.
acceptance_criteria: The Faction Status block (region/quartermaster/mage/apprentice allowances as used-of-maximum) and the Declared Attitudes block (default attitude plus the factions declared at each level) are parsed from the report and exposed to the TypeScript side; a faction view shows those alongside the faction name, id, types and unclaimed silver; a report lacking either block still parses and the view degrades rather than breaking; the real f95 and f73 turn-71 fixtures are covered by tests

title: Toggle to hide problems in the region panel
description:
## Problem

The `Problems` section sits at the top of the region panel body, above the region facts
(`packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionPanel.tsx:71`). When a hex carries several order
diagnostics the list grows and pushes population, tax base, wages, products and the rest of
the region info down out of view, so the user has to scroll past problems they have already
read to reach the numbers they came for.

## Scope

- Add a toggle that hides the Problems section in the region panel while leaving the rest of
  the panel in place.
- The toggle must stay visible when the section is hidden, and it should say how many problems
  are hidden, so the user can never lose track of unresolved diagnostics. The header `actions`
  slot on `CollapsiblePanel` is the natural place for it.
- When there are no problems for the hex the toggle should not appear at all — the section
  already renders nothing in that case.
- Persist the choice the same way panel collapse is persisted, in `workspaceStore`
  (`Persisted` picks `collapsed`/`layers`/`badges`; add the new flag to that set and to
  `reconcile`), so the preference survives a reload.

## Out of scope

- Any change to how diagnostics are computed, ordered or navigated.
- Toggles for other sections of the region panel, or for other panels.

## Validation

- `pnpm test` (unit tests for `RegionPanel` and `workspaceStore`)
- `pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck`
- Manual: select a hex with several diagnostics, hide problems, confirm the region facts move
  up to the top of the body; reload and confirm the choice stuck; select a clean hex and
  confirm no toggle is shown.
acceptance_criteria: A control in the region panel hides the Problems section and shows the region facts at the top of the panel body; the control remains visible with a count of the hidden problems; it is absent when the hex has no problems; the choice persists across a reload

title: A hex named only by a neighbour's exits is forgotten next turn
description:
## Summary

A hex known only from a neighbour's exits disappears from the map as soon as the unit that saw it
moves away. Load turn X and the unvisited neighbour A,B is drawn; load turn X+1 with the unit
elsewhere and A,B is gone, along with everything the report already told us about it.

The map forgets sighted-but-unvisited ground, so it shrinks back to the fringe of wherever the
faction currently stands rather than accumulating. That is the opposite of what the region-sightings
store exists to do.

## Problem

`buildHexMapModel` (`packages/shared/src/hexMapModel.ts:203`) assembles the map from three passes,
weakest knowledge first so stronger overwrites it:

1. `named` — hexes taken from `parsed.regions[].exits`, i.e. **the current report only**
   (`hexMapModel.ts:212-233`)
2. `stale` — hexes from the stored sightings of earlier turns (`hexMapModel.ts:235-254`)
3. `current` — hexes in this turn's report (`hexMapModel.ts:256-267`)

Pass 1 reads the current report and nothing else. Pass 2 reads stored sightings, and those only ever
cover visited regions: `region_sightings` in `crates/core/src/report/sighting.rs:40` maps
`report.regions` and nothing more, so an exit-only neighbour is never written as a sighting of its
own.

So a `named` hex lives exactly as long as the report that named it is the one on screen. Nothing
carries it into the next turn.

The persistence layer is not at fault and needs no change. `upsert_region_sightings`
(`crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs:1221`) is cumulative — it upserts on
`excluded.last_seen_turn >= region_sightings.last_seen_turn` and never deletes — so visited hexes
accumulate correctly. Only the exit-only ones were never offered to it.

## The fact is already stored

No schema change or migration is needed, and no data has been lost.

`RegionSighting.payload_json` is the whole `ReportRegion` serialized
(`sighting.rs:55`, pinned by `the_payload_is_the_whole_region`), and `ReportRegion` carries its
`exits` (`crates/core/src/report/model.rs:163`). `toStoredRegions`
(`packages/shared/src/gameMemory.ts:35`) passes that payload through as `StoredRegion.region`.

Every exit ever seen is therefore already sitting in the store, attached to the visited region that
named it. `buildHexMapModel` simply never walks `stored.region.exits` — only `parsed.regions[].exits`.

## Scope

- Pass 1 of `buildHexMapModel` should draw on the exits of stored regions as well as those of the
  current report, so a hex named in an earlier turn stays named.
- Decide what such a hex carries, and pin it with a test. Two questions the implementer must settle
  with the navigator rather than guess:
  - **`lastSeenTurn` and `ageInTurns`.** A `named` hex currently carries `null` for both
    (`hexMapModel.ts:225-226`). A hex named three turns ago is a weaker claim than one named this
    turn, and the fade and the stale cap are built on exactly that distinction.
  - **Precedence among competing exits.** Two stored regions from different turns can name the same
    hex with different terrain. The most recent naming is the obvious winner, but the current
    `if (byKey.has(key)) continue` keeps the *first* one encountered, which is arbitrary once
    stored regions join the loop.
- Keep the existing precedence intact: a visited hex must still beat a named one, and a current
  region must still beat a stored sighting.

## Out of scope

- Writing exit-only hexes as sightings of their own. The fact is already stored inside the visited
  region's payload; adding a second, weaker row for the same hex would need a migration and a rule
  for which row wins, to recover something already in hand.
- How an unsurveyed hex is drawn. `ah-rgp` settled the wash and the unsurveyed rim; this bead is
  about *whether the hex is on the map at all*, not what it looks like once it is.
- Map export (`mapExport.ts`), beyond whatever falls out of the model change.

## Validation

- A unit test in `hexMapModel.test.ts`, alongside the two that already cover named hexes
  (`marks a neighbour named only by an exit as known by name`, `lets a stored sighting override a
  hex merely named by an exit`): build a model from a turn X+1 report that does not name A,B, with a
  stored region from turn X whose exits do, and assert A,B is present and `named`.
- Manually with two consecutive real reports: load turn X, note an unvisited neighbour at the fringe,
  load turn X+1 with the unit moved away, and confirm the hex is still drawn.
- `pnpm run test` and the smoke suite stay green; the existing precedence tests must not need
  editing.
acceptance_criteria: A hex named by the exits of a region seen in an earlier turn is still drawn as a named hex after the unit that saw it has moved away and the next turn is loaded; a visited hex still beats a named one and a current region still beats a stored sighting; covered by a test in hexMapModel.test.ts
close_reason: Delivered in PR #149 (squash a8ba263): named hexes now come from remembered regions' exits as well as the report on screen

title: One gate at a time, machine-wide
description:
playwright.config.ts records its own measurement: one worker already drives this machine to about 280% CPU, and two workers broke both interactivity guards, because a test that measures how long the main thread is blocked measures contention instead.

N agents each running pnpm check reproduces exactly that, off-config. With retries: 1 the likely outcome is a flaky red that an agent then classifies as infrastructure and re-runs for free under its own rules - so either the loop burns wall-clock, or a retry-green means an agent merged on a measurement it never actually satisfied.

The gate takes an exclusive machine-wide lock so agents queue instead of contending. The same lock incidentally serialises cargo on the shared build directory.
acceptance_criteria:
pnpm check (at minimum test:smoke and test:pwa) acquires an exclusive lock before running and releases it afterwards, including on failure.
A crashed holder cannot deadlock the others.
Two agents running the gate at once produce two sequential runs, both honest.

title: Roads do not shrink with the map when zooming out
description:
## Summary

Zoomed far out, roads stop being lines and become blobs: the mark is wider than the hex it belongs
to. Reported against Miniature World and Beveled Tile, but the cause is shared and **every theme has
it** — they differ only in degree.

Each theme's `RoadLayer` draws a spoke from the hex centre along `ROAD_VECTORS[direction]`, scaled by
`HEX_RADIUS * 0.87` (0.83 in Beveled Tile). The **length** is therefore hex-relative and shrinks with
the world transform. The **width** is not: every road line carries
`vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke"`, which pins the stroke to a constant number of screen pixels at
any zoom. Nothing in any theme divides a road width by the scale or expresses it in fractions of
`HEX_RADIUS`, and the CSS road classes set colour only, never width — the JSX `strokeWidth` is the
whole story.

At `MIN_STEP = -8` the scale is 0.25 (`mapViewport.ts:35-37,78-80`), so an 18-unit hex is 4.5px on
screen and a spoke is about 3.9px long:

| theme | road stroke (constant screen px) | spoke at min zoom | width ÷ length |
|---|---|---|---|
| classic | 7 | 3.9px | ~1.8× |
| miniatureWorld | 5 | 3.9px | ~1.3× |
| beveledTile | 4 | 3.7px | ~1.1× |
| cartographersTable | 4 casing + 1.4 dash | 3.9px | ~1.0× |
| emblemAndDots | 3.4 | 3.9px | ~0.87× |
| tacticalHud | 2 | 3.9px | ~0.51× |

It reads worst at far zoom because the zoom-band CSS deliberately hides labels, pips, chips and
glyphs there while **keeping** roads (each theme.css says so — e.g. beveledTile "far keeps the tile,
its bevel and the roads"). So the fattest thing on screen is the only thing left on screen.

## Scope

- The six `RoadLayer` functions: `classic/index.tsx:58`, `cartographersTable/index.tsx:168`,
  `beveledTile/index.tsx:179`, `emblemAndDots/index.tsx:137`, `tacticalHud/index.tsx:159`,
  `miniatureWorld/index.tsx:216`.
- Agreed target: **a road keeps its proportion to the hex at every zoom.** In this codebase that
  means dropping `vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke"` from the road marks and expressing the width in
  fractions of `HEX_RADIUS`, which is the rule `mapThemes/geometry.ts:4-6` already states for marks:
  "in fractions of HEX_RADIUS rather than in absolute pixels". Each theme keeps its own relative
  weight — Tactical HUD's road stays the thinnest, Miniature World's the heaviest.
- Regression test modelled on the one that already pins the opposite behaviour for the fog lattice,
  `tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts:2011` ("the unexplored lattice keeps a constant hairline at every
  zoom"). That test asserts computed `stroke-width × --map-scale === 1` screen pixel. A road wants
  the mirror of it: computed `stroke-width` constant in **user** units across zoom steps, so its
  screen width falls with the scale. Assert it at rest, zoomed in, and at `MIN_STEP`.
- No theme currently has any test asserting a road's width or its scaling — the road tests only
  count lines and check for dashes. Whatever shape the fix takes, that gap is what let this ship.

## Two things the fix has to decide, not assume

1. **Does a road still read at far zoom once it shrinks?** The far band keeps roads precisely
   because they are the last legible structure. A width that is a true fraction of the hex is about
   1px on screen at `MIN_STEP`. If that turns out to be too faint, the honest answer is a floor
   expressed against the hex (never wider than some share of it) rather than a return to a constant
   screen width. Look at it before choosing.
2. **The route overlay is also non-scaling** (`MapCanvas.tsx:736,744` — a 5px casing and a 3px line),
   and Classic's road width of 7 was tuned explicitly against it, per the comment at
   `classic/index.tsx:52-57`: wide enough that "whether a path runs along a road or misses it stays
   legible at every zoom". If roads scale and the route overlay does not, that relationship inverts
   somewhere in the zoom range. Decide whether the overlay follows the roads.

## Out of scope

- Labels, pips, chips and the fog hairline, which are constant-screen-size deliberately and have
  their own zoom-band rules.
- Any change to road *placement* or to which hexes report roads.
- Classic, if `ah-xde` (removing that theme) has landed first — it is the worst offender at 7px, so
  the order of these two beads decides whether it is worth touching.

## Validation

- `pnpm test` — the theme road tests, plus whatever unit-level assertion the fix adds.
- `pnpm test:smoke` — both shells, including the new road-scaling test.
- `pnpm check` before the PR.
- By hand, and this is the part that actually answers it: open a hex with roads in Miniature World
  and Beveled Tile, zoom to `MIN_STEP`, and confirm a road reads as a line within its hex rather
  than a blob across it — then zoom to `MAX_STEP` and confirm it has not become a slab.
design: Target agreed with the navigator: a road keeps its proportion to the hex at every zoom. The cause is vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke" on every road line, which pins the width to screen pixels while the spoke length stays hex-relative - so the two diverge as the map scales. Reported for Miniature World and Beveled Tile; investigation found all six themes affected, Classic worst at 7px against a 3.9px spoke at minimum zoom. Two questions are left open on purpose because they need to be looked at rather than reasoned about: whether a proportional road still reads at far zoom, where the zoom band keeps roads as the last visible structure, and whether the route overlay - also non-scaling, and what Classic's width was tuned against - should follow the roads.
acceptance_criteria:
At MIN_STEP a road reads as a line inside its hex rather than a mark wider than the hex, in every theme that ships.
A road's width is expressed against HEX_RADIUS rather than in constant screen pixels, so its on-screen width falls with the map scale.
A smoke test pins the scaling across zoom steps, mirroring the fog lattice's constant-hairline test rather than repeating it.
Each theme keeps its own relative road weight - the thin ones stay thin, the heavy ones stay heavy.
pnpm check passes.
notes:
Far-zoom question answered by looking, not reasoning: screenshots of all five themes at the fixture's road hex (1:7,53 and the mountain at 1:7,51), at step -4 and at MIN_STEP.

At -4 (the far band) every theme's road reads cleanly as a line inside its hex - the bug is gone and nothing was lost. At MIN_STEP (scale 0.25) Miniature World (1.25px), Beveled Tile and Cartographer's casing (1.0px) are still visible; Emblem and Dots (0.85px) is faint; Tactical HUD (0.5px) and Cartographer's dash (0.35px) are close to invisible. No road disappears outright across the band, so NO FLOOR was added, per the agreed rule. The fallback if it proves too faint in use is max(width, 1px / var(--map-scale)) in a style declaration - noted in tacticalHud/index.tsx beside its constant.

Second open question, decided with the navigator: the route overlay follows the roads (casing 5, line 3, risk outline 2, all now in hex units). The selection and focus rings on the same hexagon stay screen-constant, being chrome rather than ground.

Side effect worth watching in use: dash patterns were measured in the non-scaling space before and are hex-relative now, so at MIN_STEP the dotted route is ~1.5px on/off - the solid-vs-dotted distinction is still there but subtle.
close_reason: Delivered in PR #144. Roads in all five themes and the route overlay (casing, line, risk outline) now take their width from radii() instead of vectorEffect='non-scaling-stroke', so they shrink with the hex. Far-zoom question answered by screenshot, no floor needed; see the bead notes.

title: Remove the Classic map theme
description:
## Summary

Remove the **Classic** map theme. It is the map as it looked before the five designed themes
arrived, and it is now the least of them; keeping it costs a directory of drawing code, a share of
every theme-wide change, and a slot in the settings picker.

Classic is not an ordinary registry entry, which is what makes this more than a deletion. It is
**`DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID`**, and it is the hard-coded last resort inside `getMapTheme` for a registry
that contains no default at all. Both have to move before the directory can go.

**Cartographer's Table becomes the new default** (decided with the navigator).

## Scope

- Delete `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/classic/` — `index.tsx` and `classic.test.tsx`.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/index.ts`: drop the import and the `MAP_THEMES` entry,
  point `DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID` at `cartographers-table`, and replace the `?? classic` last resort in
  `getMapTheme` with the new default's module. Update the file header comment, which currently
  describes the order as "the map as it was, then the five designs".
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/index.test.tsx` — the registry tests name Classic
  directly, including the fallback-of-last-resort case.
- Persisted settings need no migration code: `knownMapTheme` in
  `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts:142` already answers `DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID` for any id the
  registry does not know, so a stored `"classic"` moves to the new default on the next load. This is
  worth an explicit test rather than an assumption — a stored `"classic"` must land on
  Cartographer's Table, not throw and not render nothing.
- `tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts` — five assertions name `classic` or `map-theme-classic`, including
  the picker's default value and a test that switches away from Classic and back to it. They need
  rewriting around two themes that still ship.
- Docs, rewritten against the new default rather than merely struck: `docs/ui/hex-rendering.md`
  describes what is drawn largely in terms of what Classic draws (its opening note, the "not yet
  implemented" list at the foot); `docs/ui/README.md` says "All six ship: Classic, plus the five
  designs" and carries a Classic Commander layout section; `docs/ui/map-themes.md` is the registry's
  own reference.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/hexView.ts:53` mentions "the classic hull names" — that
  is Atlantis ship vocabulary, not the theme. Leave it.

## Out of scope

- Any change to the other five themes' drawing.
- A migration dialog or a notice telling the user their theme changed. The silent fallback is the
  agreed behaviour.

## Validation

- `pnpm test` — registry tests, the new stored-`"classic"` fallback test, settings store tests.
- `pnpm test:smoke` — both shells; the map theme picker walk is the one that moves most.
- `pnpm check` before the PR.
- By hand: open the app with `"classic"` already in `atlantis-hud-settings`, confirm the map draws
  as Cartographer's Table and the picker shows it, and confirm the picker no longer offers Classic.
design: Cartographer's Table becomes the new default, chosen with the navigator as the most map-like of the remaining five and the next in registry order. No migration code is written: knownMapTheme already answers DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID for an unknown id, so a stored "classic" moves across on the next load - the point is to test that rather than assume it. Docs are rewritten in the same bead rather than split off, because hex-rendering.md describes the map in terms of what Classic draws and would otherwise document a theme that no longer exists.
acceptance_criteria:
The settings picker no longer offers Classic, and packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/classic/ is gone.
DEFAULT_MAP_THEME_ID is cartographers-table, and getMapTheme's last resort for a registry without a default no longer mentions Classic.
A settings blob holding mapTheme "classic" loads as Cartographer's Table rather than failing or drawing nothing, pinned by a test.
docs/ui/hex-rendering.md, docs/ui/README.md and docs/ui/map-themes.md describe the themes that actually ship, with the rendering prose rewritten against the new default.
pnpm check passes.

title: Refresh the beads issues export at pre-push instead of on every commit
description:
`.beads/issues.jsonl` is a generated file that is committed so the backlog is diffable in the repo.
Keeping it fresh is currently an obligation on every commit: `export.auto: true` in
`.beads/config.yaml` makes the bd pre-commit hook write it, and the beads-workflow skill's
end-of-session checklist asks for `bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl` by hand. Auto-export is
throttled to once a minute, and it has already committed a snapshot that still held a bead deleted
minutes earlier (#132 documented the trap and the `git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l` check
that catches it). Two sessions in a row have then ended with the export knowingly out of date,
because refreshing it means a commit straight to `main`.

Move the obligation to push time, where it is needed once per branch instead of once per commit and
where nothing can be pushed stale.

## Scope

- A repo-owned gate that runs from `.beads/hooks/pre-push`, below the `BEADS INTEGRATION` markers
  so `bd hooks install` preserves it (`bd hooks install --help`: user content outside the markers
  survives installs and upgrades).
- The gate exports the database to a temporary file and compares it with the committed
  `.beads/issues.jsonl`. Equal: the push proceeds and the gate says nothing. Different: the gate
  writes the fresh export, commits that one file as `chore(beads): refresh the issues export`, and
  aborts the push with a message saying the commit was made and to push again.
- A pre-push hook cannot amend or extend the commits being pushed — the refs are already computed —
  so the refresh is a new commit and the push is aborted rather than rewritten. No `--force` is
  ever needed.
- `export.auto` goes to `false`, which is beads' own default, so no throttled snapshot can reach a
  commit again.
- The gate is inert when it cannot do its job: no `bd` on PATH, no `.beads` directory, or a
  `bd export` that fails must let the push through rather than block it. A tooling convenience must
  not stand between the player and their remote.
- The beads-workflow skill loses the per-session export step and gains a short description of the
  gate, replacing the trap section's manual verification advice.
- Repo tooling has no test home today, so the gate's decision logic is written to be unit-testable
  and a root vitest project is wired up for `scripts/`, run by `pnpm run check` and by the CI
  `checks` job.

## Out of scope

- Whether the export is committed at all — that question was settled in favour of keeping it.
- The Dolt remote and `bd dolt push`, which stay exactly as they are.
- The other four bd hooks.
- Any CI check that validates the export server-side.

## Validation

- Unit tests for the gate: unchanged export, changed export, missing `.beads`, absent `bd`, and a
  failing `bd export`.
- An end-to-end shell exercise in a throwaway git repo with a bare remote and a stubbed `bd` on
  PATH: a stale export aborts the first push with the refresh commit in place, and the second push
  succeeds with the fresh file in it.
- `pnpm run check` and the CI gate.
- Manually, on this branch: with a deliberately stale JSONL, `git push` refuses once, leaves the
  refresh commit, and succeeds on the retry.
acceptance_criteria:
A repo-owned gate runs from .beads/hooks/pre-push, below the beads markers, and survives bd hooks install.
A push whose committed .beads/issues.jsonl matches a fresh bd export proceeds silently.
A push whose committed export is stale is aborted, with the fresh export committed alone as chore(beads): refresh the issues export, and the retry succeeds.
No push is ever rewritten or needs --force.
export.auto is false in .beads/config.yaml.
The gate lets the push through when bd is absent, .beads is missing, or bd export fails.
The beads-workflow skill drops the per-session export step and describes the gate instead.
The gate's logic is covered by unit tests that run in pnpm run check and in CI.

title: Remember map zoom level and focus hex across reloads
description:
The map view resets when a game is reloaded. The user has to zoom and pan back to where they were working.

Goal: persist the map viewport per game so reloading restores the previous view.

Scope:
- Persist current zoom level and the focused/centered hex
- Restore them when the same game is loaded again
- Fall back to the current default view when no saved state exists (e.g. first load of a game)

Acceptance criteria:
- Reloading a game restores the zoom level and centered hex from the previous session
- Viewport state is stored per game, so switching between games does not mix up views

title: Map forgets known-but-never-occupied hexes once no unit can see them
description:
When a unit moves away, the map stops showing hexes that were known only from that unit's line of sight. Only the hex the unit itself occupied earlier remains on the map; the surrounding 6 hexes (e.g. ocean hexes seen from a fleet jump but never entered) disappear.

Expected: once a hex has been observed in any report, it stays on the map as known terrain (with the data from the last turn it was observed), even when no unit can currently see it.

Actual: only hexes a unit actually occupied are remembered; adjacent observed-only hexes are dropped when they leave current visibility.

Acceptance criteria:
- Hexes observed from an adjacent unit remain visible on the map after the unit leaves
- Remembered hexes show the terrain and data from the most recent turn they were observed
- Currently visible vs remembered hexes remain distinguishable (see ah-rgp)
close_reason: Duplicate of ah-ctf, delivered in PR #149 (squash a8ba263). All three acceptance criteria met: namings now come from remembered regions' exits, the most recent naming wins, and named hexes keep the ah-rgp unsurveyed rim. No work was ever committed under this bead - its branch held zero commits.

title: Option to keep the long order format when exporting orders
description:
Exported orders come out in the short format only. The server's own unit description — name,
flags, weight, capacity, skills and what the unit can study, wrapped over as many `;` lines as it
takes — is dropped the moment a report's template becomes an editable document
(`stripUnitComments` in `packages/shared/src/ordersDocument.ts`, called once from
`documentFor` in `packages/shared/src/orderDraft.ts:113`), and `exportOrders`
(`packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx:1526`) writes that stripped document straight out.

Dropping the descriptions from the editor was deliberate (#37): the unit panel already says all of
it, and on a unit with no orders yet the description is the whole block. But the exported file is
read elsewhere — kept as a record of the turn, diffed against the next one, or read by a human
without this application in front of them — and there the long format is what makes a bare
`unit 793` legible:

```
unit 793
;Three of Five (793), behind, revealing faction, leader [LEAD]. Weight:
;  10. Capacity: 0/0/15/0. Skills: observation [OBSE] 1 (35), force
;  [FORC] 1 (35), pattern [PATT] 1 (30), spirit [SPIR] 1 (30), gate
;  lore [GATE] 1 (30), fire [FIRE] 1 (30), combat [COMB] 3 (180). Can
;  Study: earthquake [EQUA], force shield [FSHI], energy shield [ESHI],
;  spirit shield [SSHI], magical healing [MHEA], farsight [FARS], mind
;  reading [MIND], weather lore [WEAT], earth lore [EART], necromancy
;  [NECR], demon lore [DEMO], illusion [ILLU], artifact lore [ARTI].
@study obse
```

So the option belongs on the export, not on the editor: the descriptions stay out of the panel the
player writes in, and go back into the file on the way out when asked for.

## Scope

- An option on the orders export that puts the server's long-format unit descriptions back into the
  exported text. Default off, so today's output is unchanged unless the player asks.
- The descriptions are recovered from the report's own template (`parsed.ordersTemplate`), matched
  per `unit` block, rather than kept in the document — the document must stay as it is, or the
  editor regains the clutter #37 removed.
- Each unit's description is written directly under its `unit` line, above the player's orders, in
  the server's own wrapping, byte for byte as the report carried it.
- Units the template has no description for (a unit formed this turn by the player) simply get
  none; the export must not fail or invent one.
- The player's own `;` notes in the draft are untouched and not duplicated.
- The same option and the same output on both shells — web download and desktop save alike.

## Out of scope

- Any change to what the editor shows, or to `stripUnitComments` at seed time.
- The `Orders Template (Long Format):` banner and the region `;*** ... ***` banners — this is about
  unit descriptions only.
- The map export in `crates/core/src/report/export.rs`, which is a separate path.
- Reformatting or re-wrapping descriptions; they go out as they came in.

## Validation

- `pnpm run check` and `cargo test` (or `pnpm run check` alone if the change stays in TypeScript).
- A unit test over the committed turn 71 fixture: export with the option on, and every `unit` line
  that has a description in the template is followed by exactly those `;` lines, in that order.
- The same export with the option off is byte for byte what is exported today.
- Round trip: an export written with the option on, imported back as a draft, seeds a document with
  the descriptions stripped again — no accumulation.
- A smoke test exercising the checkbox from the orders panel, on web and desktop-shell.
- Manually: export a turn with the option on, and read the file — a leader's eight-line description
  should be intact and correctly indented.
acceptance_criteria:
The orders export offers an option, default off, that writes the server's long-format unit descriptions into the exported file.
With the option off the exported text is byte for byte what is exported today.
With the option on, every unit whose template block carried a description has those ';' lines directly under its 'unit' line, verbatim and in order, above the player's orders.
A unit with no description in the template exports without one and without error.
The player's own ';' notes are neither dropped nor duplicated.
Re-importing an export written with the option on seeds a document with the descriptions stripped, so they do not accumulate.
The option and its output are the same on the web download and the desktop save.

title: Make terrain of undiscovered hexes more visible on the map
description:
Undiscovered (not yet explored) hexes render their terrain image so heavily whitened/faded that the terrain type is not distinguishable at a glance. There are thin differences in the image background, but they are too subtle.

Goal: make it clear at a glance what terrain an undiscovered hex has, while still keeping a clear visual distinction between discovered and undiscovered hexes.

Ideas to consider:
- Reduce the whitening/desaturation amount for undiscovered hexes
- Keep the fade but add a stronger terrain-colored tint
- Use a distinct marker (outline style, hatching, reduced opacity instead of whitening) for the discovered/undiscovered distinction instead of washing out the terrain

Acceptance criteria:
- Terrain type of an undiscovered hex is recognizable at a glance in all map themes
- Discovered vs undiscovered hexes remain visually distinguishable
close_reason: Delivered in PR #143 (squash a1fcafa), which was merged 2026-08-12 but left the bead open. Both criteria met: the fog wash dropped 0.78 -> 0.40 so terrain reads at a glance (NAMED_FOG_OPACITY in mapHexView.ts), and the discovered/undiscovered distinction moved to a per-theme unsurveyed rim, pinned for every theme by the registry-wide test in mapThemes/index.test.tsx.

title: Max number of units settable from the units-in-hex pane
description:
It should be possible to increase/decrease the number of units that are shown in the units-in-hex pane by clicking a + or - located to the right on the top bar of the pane. There shall also be a text indicating what the max units shown are, as this may be more than the hex currently has.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The units-in-hex pane's top bar carries + and - controls on its right-hand side.
- Clicking + or - raises or lowers the maximum number of units listed, and the list updates immediately.
- The top bar shows the current maximum, including when the hex holds fewer units than that.
- The chosen maximum survives a reload.

title: Toggle badges on/off in the map display
description:
It should be possible to toggle different badges on/off in the map display to reduce cluttering.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each kind of badge drawn on the map can be turned on and off independently.
- The map redraws immediately when a badge kind is toggled.
- The chosen set of visible badges survives a reload.

title: Commit a second turn so multi-step routes can be proved on real data
description:
## Summary

Commit a second real turn for one faction, so that routes longer than one step can be proved against
real data rather than only against synthetic corridors.

## Problem

Issue #8 built a map that accumulates across turns, and it works: the core merges remembered regions
with the current report, the current turn wins where they disagree, and both platforms store and
read back region sightings. All of that is unit-tested.

None of it can be demonstrated end to end, because the repository holds exactly one report per
faction: neworigins-3.0.0-f73-t2.rep for faction 73 and neworigins-3.0.0-f95-t71.rep for faction 95.

A single report cannot support a route longer than one step. It describes the hexes the faction
stood in and names their neighbours, but a named hex describes no exits of its own, so the graph
stops at the fringe. With the committed fixtures, every route the planner produces is one step.

Multi-step, multi-month, road and flight behaviour is therefore covered only against small synthetic
reports built in the tests. Those are honest tests, but they are our own fixtures rather than the
game's output, and they cannot catch a disagreement between what we think a report says and what one
actually says.

Fabricating a second turn was deliberately avoided during #8: inventing game data and committing it
as a fixture would make every test built on it worthless as evidence.

## Scope

- Commit a genuine second turn for faction 95, ideally adjacent in time to turn 71
- Add an acceptance test that imports both turns and plans a route crossing ground the later report
  does not describe
- Extend the smoke suite so the multi-step case is exercised in a browser, not only in the core

## Acceptance criteria

- Two turns of one faction are committed under tests/fixtures/reports
- A test plans a route of more than one step over the accumulated map, with a cost read from the
  reports by hand
- The stale map state is exercised, since it becomes reachable only once a hex is remembered from an
  earlier turn than the current one

## Validation

    cargo test --workspace
    pnpm run check

## Dependencies / Links

- Main issue: #1
- Follows: #8

## Note

This one needs a human: the report has to come from a real game.

title: Turn-to-turn diffs for units, regions, and orders
description:
## Summary

Compare two imported turns of a game and see what changed: units gained/lost/moved, region changes, and how the orders differ.

## Problem

The app keeps every imported turn in storage, but the player can only ever look at the latest one. Between turns the real questions are "what changed since last month?" and "what did I order last time?" — today that means opening two report text files side by side.

## Scope

- An API to enumerate the imported turns of a game (`listImportedTurns` through core-persistence, the WASM and Tauri adapters, and the shared `CoreClient`), since today only "a known turn number" or "latest" can be loaded.
- Loading a second turn alongside the current one for comparison (the app currently holds exactly one parsed report in memory).
- A diff view for a chosen turn pair surfacing adds/removes/changes for units, regions, and orders.

## Out of scope

- Diffing more than two turns at once, or cross-game comparison.
- Changes to report parsing or order validation.

## Acceptance criteria

- The user can pick two imported turns of the current game.
- The diff view lists units added, removed, and changed between the pair.
- The diff view lists region changes between the pair.
- The diff view shows how the orders drafts differ between the pair.

## Validation

- Import two consecutive turn reports with known differences; open the diff view and verify each known difference is surfaced and nothing is falsely reported.
- Vitest coverage for the diff computation modules; a Playwright smoke walk of the diff view on both web and desktop-shell projects.

## Dependencies / Links

- Broken out of issue 9 (Productivity UX), where it was originally a scope bullet; deferred to its own deliverable.
- Storage substrate already exists: `imported_turns` table keyed by game/faction/turn in `crates/core-persistence`.

title: Load multiple reports
description:
It shall be possible to load multiple reports in one go. The application shall then look at the headers of all reports to figure out in which order the reports shall be loaded. It shall be possible to load both your own and allies reports in one go.

While we are at it, the menu option for loading orders shall be changed to "Import".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Several report files can be selected and imported in one action.
- The application reads the turn number from each report header and loads them in turn order, regardless of the order they were selected in.
- Own-faction and ally reports can be imported together in the same action.
- The menu option for loading reports reads "Import".
close_reason: Delivered in PR #133: batch import of several reports, ordered by header turn, with the load control renamed Import

title: Record beads CLI traps in the beads-workflow skill
description:
Three beads behaviours bit during the #126 migration and are not obvious from the CLI help. Record them in the beads-workflow skill so the next session does not rediscover them.

- The pre-commit auto-export can write a stale snapshot: a commit picked up a JSONL still containing a throwaway bead that had already been deleted.
- `bd config set` accepts unknown keys silently, so a mistyped key reads as success; probing also rewrote a commented-out default in `.beads/config.yaml` and stripped its trailing newline.
- The `owner` field is taken from `git config user.email` at creation and has no override; `--actor` sets `created_by` only, and `--assignee` is a separate field.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `.claude/skills/beads-workflow/SKILL.md` carries a section covering all three behaviours.
- The export trap names the verification command that catches it.

title: Plan sea movement for fleets
description:
## Summary

Plan sea movement: routes for units aboard a fleet, emitting SAIL rather than MOVE.

## Problem

The planner handles land movement only. A unit standing in an ocean hex - which is what a unit
aboard a fleet looks like in a report - is refused with "the sea is in the way", and so is any
destination across water. That is correct for what #8 built, and useless for a faction that sails.

The rules make sailing a second system rather than a variation:

- A fleet has its own speed, stated per ship on the data page: a Longship moves 4 hexes per month, a
  Raft 2, a Galleon 4
- "For a fleet to enter any region only costs one movement point", so the terrain premium that
  applies to riding and walking units does not apply at sea
- Sailing needs a total of N levels of sailing skill among the crew, stated per ship
- A fleet has a cargo capacity, which the scraper already records as cargoCapacity
- Guards behave differently: a fleet enters a guarded region and is then stopped, where a land unit
  is prevented from entering at all

## Scope

- A Sail movement mode, with speed taken from the ship rather than from the unit
- Flat terrain cost at sea, per the quoted rule
- Recognising that a unit is aboard a fleet it can actually sail, including the skill requirement
- Emitting SAIL orders rather than MOVE
- Refusing a sea route with a named reason when the crew cannot sail the ship

## Out of scope

- Combat at sea
- Building or repairing ships

## Acceptance criteria

- A unit aboard a fleet can be given a sea route with a cost and a month breakdown
- A crew without the sailing skill the ship requires is refused with that as the reason
- Land units are unaffected

## Notes

Two loose ends from #8 belong here. MovementMode has no Sail variant, deliberately. And
crates/core/src/movement/mode.rs has a can_swim function that nothing outside its own test calls -
this ruleset's water rule exempts only flight from needing a ship, so swimming currently decides
nothing; it should either be used here or deleted.

## Dependencies / Links

- Main issue: #1
- Out of scope of: #8

title: Import lots of reports
description:
There are plenty of old Borg reports that could be imported to the code base to potentially be used for testing. This issue should cover importing them into the code base in a structured way and they should be used by later issues.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The Borg reports are committed under a documented location in the repository.
- File naming encodes game, faction and turn so a test can select a report without opening it.
- A short document records where the reports came from and what they may be used for.
